```json
{
  "winner": "A",
  "reasons": [
    "B has a hard regulatory gate that A lacks. B's own brief says IRS e-file Provider authorization 'can take up to 45 days (IRS Pub 3112)', which eats half the 90-day window before a full filer can ship. A's baseline product (deadline tracking, alerts, dashboard) needs no license or authorization to sell.",
    "A has sourced evidence that people pay for tracking alone, without the hard rule-change data layer. ClearBot's Essential tier is 'tracking only' at $500/location/yr, and Expiration Reminder and RenewalTracker publish $49/mo tiers. A solo operator can therefore launch a narrow, lower-liability product and still match an existing paid offering.",
    "A's cited demand quotes describe the tracking problem directly: an engineer keeping a spreadsheet of multi-state renewal dates, and a therapist weighing a $440 renewal. B's cited quotes describe general PFIC and FATCA distress. None shows a buyer looking for a cheaper or better DIY filer than the existing $119–$199 tools.",
    "B carries higher liability per error. Its brief states that 'PFIC/FBAR/FATCA errors can cost customers tens of thousands of dollars', and that falls on a brand-new one-person product competing against incumbents with 165k and 100k users. A also has trust and liability risk, but its brief treats this as an open question that insurance or ToS might address, not as a launch blocker.",
    "A's subscription pricing ($29–99/mo) and year-round B2B pain can produce a paying customer at any time of year. B's brief gives no evidence on when in the year expats buy, and its pricing implies a one-time purchase per return."
  ],
  "weakest_evidence_in_loser": "B's claim of a 'validated, underserved sub-segment' is inferred only from the fact that incumbents charge upsells for investor/PFIC features. No sourced evidence shows investor expats are dissatisfied with Expatfile, MyExpatTaxes, or H&R Block, or would switch to a new entrant. The demand quotes show pain about PFIC rules and attorney remediation costs (e.g., '$50K'), not unmet demand for another DIY filer.",
  "confidence_note": "Moderate confidence. Both ideas are crowded, high-trust compliance categories, and neither brief shows direct willingness to pay a new entrant. A's own demand evidence points to spreadsheet inertia, and its CPL figures ($87–200) come from a source the brief flags as possibly AI-aggregated. So A is not strong on its own terms. The decision rests mainly on B's 45-day e-file authorization gate and its more severe error liability, both of which are well-sourced obstacles to reaching a paying customer within 90 days. If B were narrowed to a standalone PFIC calculator that needs no e-file authorization, the comparison could tighten, but B's brief does not provide evidence for that version."
}
```
